extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents prosecuting patents)
extracted.subtask_description: Examination guidelines for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, describing the factual inquiries, search scope, rationales for obviousness, evidentiary standards, and procedural expectations for Office actions and applicant replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art is a primary Graham factual inquiry; Office personnel must obtain a thorough understanding of the invention disclosed and claimed by reading the specification, including the claims, to understand what the applicant has invented. The scope of the claimed invention must be clearly determined by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once claim scope is determined, decide what to search for and where. See MPEP §904–904.03 for search guidelines. Prior art may be in the applicant's field or reasonably pertinent to the problem; nonanalogous fields can be used if reasonably pertinent. Search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining the differences requires interpreting claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims (see MPEP §2111) and consider all claim limitations. The mere existence of differences does not establish nonobviousness; the gap may not be so great as to render the claim nonobvious to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual Graham inquiry: determine the hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the pertinent art to assess what would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider may include: type of problems encountered in the art; prior art solutions; rapidity of innovations; sophistication of the technology; and educational level of active workers. Not all factors must be present; one or more may predominate. Office personnel may rely on their own technical expertise and on references (even non-prior art) to show level of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of objective evidence/secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (secondary considerations) relevant to obviousness must be evaluated: commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, unexpected results, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be in the specification, filed with the application, or timely submitted later. Weight given is case-by-case; presence of evidence is not dispositive by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel as factfinders — requirement to articulate factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel serve as factfinders for the Graham inquiries; the underlying factual findings must be included in the written record and used to support an obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection, ensure the Office action contains explicit factual findings (e.g., state of the art, teachings of references, how a person of ordinary skill would have understood the art). These findings are necessary to support a legal conclusion of obviousness and to notify applicant of reasons for rejection per 35 U.S.C. 132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation — broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification when determining scope for obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Phillips v. AWH Corp. and MPEP §2111. Read specification and claims to understand what applicant has invented before searching/prior art comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, a preferred search will look for references that provide such teaching or suggestion if they exist (MPEP §904.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search — scope of prior art fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art can be either in the field of the applicant's endeavor or be reasonably pertinent to the particular problem with which the applicant was concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References from other fields of endeavor may be relevant, particularly where design incentives or market forces would prompt predictable variations. Do not limit search only to references addressing the patentee's problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear articulation of reasons and reasoning (no conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit explanation of why differences between prior art and claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill. Avoid unexplained reliance on 'common sense' without reasoned explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: One rationale for a conclusion of obviousness: combining prior art elements using known methods when the combination yields predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples and prior cases (KSR) to explain predictability; document why combination would be expected to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness can be found where one known element is substituted for another known element resulting in predictable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why a person of ordinary skill would have made the substitution and why the result would be predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices, methods, or products
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique that was used to improve one device to improve similar devices may be obvious if the improvement is predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the basis for expecting similar improvement in the claimed device and why the technique would be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device which is ready for improvement may support an obviousness finding when results are predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the device was 'ready for improvement' and that the technique would predictably produce the claimed result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: 'Obvious to try' with finite, predictable solutions and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' may support obviousness where there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions and a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the solutions were finite/predictable and articulate the reasonable expectation of success; mere possibility is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same or different field
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field can prompt predictable variations for use in the same or different field based on design incentives or market forces, supporting obviousness if predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document cross-field relevance and predictability; do not confine analysis to the problem the patentee was trying to solve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art to modify or combine references may support an obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although KSR discouraged rigid TSM application, TSM remains a valid rationale when present; if present, identify the teaching/suggestion/motivation or explain an alternative reasoned rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away and effect on obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art that criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution may 'teach away' and weigh against a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidence where prior art teaches away (e.g., counsels against the approach) — mere disclosure of alternatives without criticism does not constitute teaching away. Cite cases (e.g., W.L. Gore v. Garlock; In re Fulton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense and examiner expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may rely on common sense and their technical expertise as part of the obviousness analysis, including inferences and creative steps a person of ordinary skill would employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such reliance must be reasoned and explained; common sense alone cannot be an unexplained conclusory assertion. Examiners are 'persons of scientific competence' and may interpret references in light of their expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case and supporting rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: A legal concept: once Graham factual inquiries are made, Office personnel must determine whether the claimed invention would have been obvious. If a prima facie case exists, articulate the rationale(s) (TSM or other valid rationales) supporting the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of exemplary rationales is non-exhaustive; use additional rationales if properly reasoned. See MPEP §2143–§2144 for examples and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply obligations under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with an obviousness rejection, the applicant must timely and distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred on factual findings; mere assertions that a prima facie case was not established or unsupported appeals to common knowledge are insufficient and may lead to final rejection (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence submitted by applicants when reevaluating an obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may be in the specification, filed with the application, or submitted later; weigh evidence case-by-case. The burden shifts to applicant once Office establishes Graham factual findings and an obviousness conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art may be used to show level of skill or motivation even if not prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: References that postdate the invention or were not widely disseminated (and thus not prior art) may nonetheless be used to demonstrate level of ordinary skill or a motivation to combine implicit in the knowledge of one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such materials carefully to support factual findings as permitted by case law (e.g., Ex parte Erlich; National Steel Car Ltd. v. Canadian Pacific Railway).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of patent law precedent and MPEP guidance as supporting rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal precedent and long-standing MPEP guidance may be relied upon as sources of supporting rationale for obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cited Federal Circuit and Supreme Court cases (KSR, Graham, Sakraida, Adams, Anderson’s-Black Rock, etc.) and MPEP sections (e.g., §2143, §2144) for illustrative reasoning and examples.
